surveyor1.summary: Surveyor 1 was the first American spacecraft to make a gentle landing on the Moon, touching down on the Ocean of Storms on June 2, 1966. Its TV camera sent home more than 11,000 pictures and showed that the ground was firm enough for astronauts to land on. The silent lander is still standing there, and NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed it from above.

fate.label: Battery failed at its second sunset
fate.summary: Surveyor 1 survived its first freezing two-week lunar night and took more pictures when the Sun came back. Its mission ended on July 13, 1966, when its battery voltage dropped sharply just after sunset. Engineers kept checking in on it until January 7, 1967.

photo.caption: A full-size mock-up of a Surveyor lander, photographed in 1966. Surveyor 1 was built to this design.

orbit.caption: Surveyor 1 on the Ocean of Storms, seen from orbit by LRO's camera. The 3.3-meter-tall lander casts a shadow almost 15 meters long in the late-afternoon sunlight.

surveyor3.summary: Surveyor 3 landed in a small crater on the Ocean of Storms on April 20, 1967, touching down three times because its engines did not shut off in time. It used a robot scoop to dig trenches and test how firm the Moon's soil was. In 1969 the Apollo 12 astronauts landed nearby, walked over to it and took some of its parts home, but the rest of the lander is still there.

fate.label: Never woke up after the lunar night
fate.summary: Surveyor 3 worked through its first two-week lunar day. Its last data arrived on May 4, 1967, just after sunset, and it failed to come back to life after the long, freezing lunar night. In November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts removed its TV camera and other parts so scientists could study how they had changed on the Moon.

photo.caption: Apollo 12 commander Pete Conrad inspects Surveyor 3 on November 20, 1969. The lunar module Intrepid stands in the background. Photo taken by astronaut Alan Bean.

orbit.caption: Surveyor 3's landing site photographed from orbit by LRO's camera (image M137699517L).

surveyor5.summary: Surveyor 5 landed on the Sea of Tranquility on September 11, 1967, even though a leak in its engine system nearly ruined the landing. It made the first chemical test of soil on another world and sent back about 19,000 pictures. It still sits on a slope inside a small crater, about 25 km from where Apollo 11 landed less than two years later.

fate.label: Gave out after several lunar nights
fate.summary: Surveyor 5 was shut down for its first lunar night on September 24, 1967, and came back to work on October 15. It kept sending data on and off through more freezing nights until its final transmission on December 17, 1967.

photo.caption: Surveyor 5 being attached to its launch adapter before launch in 1967.

orbit.caption: Surveyor 5 inside its small crater, seen from orbit by LRO's camera and enlarged 4 times.

surveyor6.summary: Surveyor 6 landed on Sinus Medii, near the center of the Moon's near side, on November 10, 1967, to check a possible Apollo landing area. A week later it fired its engines, rose 3 to 4 meters and landed about 2.4 meters away, the first time a spacecraft ever lifted off from the Moon. It is still sitting where it came down after that hop.

fate.label: Didn't recover from the lunar night
fate.summary: Surveyor 6 stopped taking pictures a few hours after sunset on November 24, 1967, and was put into hibernation for the two-week lunar night on November 26. Engineers heard from it briefly on December 14, 1967, but it sent no useful data and was never heard from again.

photo.caption: A Surveyor test model during a drop test at Holloman Air Force Base, New Mexico, checking its landing system. Surveyor 6 used the same design.

orbit.caption: Surveyor 6 seen from orbit by LRO's camera. With the Sun just 8 degrees above the horizon, the lander casts an 18-meter-long shadow.

surveyor7.summary: Surveyor 7 was the last Surveyor and the only one to land in the bright, rugged highlands, near the young crater Tycho, on January 10, 1968. It took more than 21,000 pictures, dug into the ground with its scoop and analyzed the soil, finding that highland soil is different from the soil of the dark 'seas'. It is still parked on the blanket of rock and dust that Tycho threw out when it formed.

fate.label: Fell silent after its second lunar day
fate.summary: Like the other Surveyors, it ran on solar power and batteries that were not built for the freezing two-week lunar night. It was shut down on January 26, 1968, survived the night, and went back to work on February 12. Operations ended for good on February 21, 1968.

photo.caption: The Surveyor S-10 engineering model, a full-size test version of the lander, at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. It is set up to look like the later Surveyors, including Surveyor 7.
photo.credit: National Air and Space Museum, Smithsonian Institution (photo by Mark Avino)

orbit.caption: Surveyor 7 on the debris blanket of Tycho crater, seen from orbit by LRO's camera. The inset is zoomed in 4 times.

ranger6.summary: Ranger 6 was a robot spacecraft built to take close-up TV pictures of the Moon while diving straight into it. It flew right on target and crashed into the Sea of Tranquility on February 2, 1964, but its cameras never worked. All that is left is a small crater, which LRO's camera has photographed from orbit.

fate.label: Crashed as planned, but cameras failed
fate.summary: Rangers had no brakes or landing legs. They were built to take TV pictures all the way down until they smashed into the Moon. Ranger 6 hit its target on February 2, 1964, but its TV cameras had been damaged, probably by electrical arcing shortly after launch, so it sent back no pictures.

photo.caption: Ranger 6 on a vibration test table at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in 1963, being shaken to make sure it could survive launch.

orbit.caption: The Ranger 6 impact site in the Sea of Tranquility, photographed from orbit by LRO's camera (image M131508222R).

ranger7.summary: Ranger 7 was NASA's first successful Ranger, a robot camera ship designed to take pictures as it dove into the Moon. On July 31, 1964, it sent back 4,308 close-up photos in its final 17 minutes, far sharper than any telescope on Earth could see. It left a small crater in an area later named Mare Cognitum, 'the Sea that has become known'.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose while taking pictures
fate.summary: Rangers had no brakes or landing legs. They were built to take TV pictures all the way down until they smashed into the Moon. Ranger 7 did exactly that, hitting the Moon at about 2.6 km per second on July 31, 1964.

photo.caption: Engineers with Ranger 7 at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory on December 10, 1963.

orbit.caption: The area around the Ranger 7 impact site, seen from orbit by LRO's camera with the Sun low in the sky, which makes even small craters stand out.

ranger8.summary: Ranger 8 was a robot camera ship sent to photograph the Sea of Tranquility, a smooth area NASA was considering for the first human landings. It sent back 7,137 pictures in its final 23 minutes before crashing on February 20, 1965. Its small impact crater lies about 70 km from where Apollo 11 landed four years later.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose while taking pictures
fate.summary: Rangers had no brakes or landing legs. They were built to take TV pictures all the way down until they smashed into the Moon. Ranger 8 photographed the Sea of Tranquility until it was destroyed on impact on February 20, 1965, as planned.

photo.caption: Ranger 7 at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in 1963. Ranger 8 was built to the same design (Rangers 6 to 9 were near-identical).

orbit.caption: The Ranger 8 impact site in the Sea of Tranquility, photographed from orbit by LRO's camera (image M116154252).

ranger9.summary: Ranger 9 was the last Ranger, sent to photograph Alphonsus, a large crater where scientists thought there might once have been volcanic activity. As it fell on March 24, 1965, TV networks showed its pictures live with the words 'Live from the Moon' on screen. It sent 5,814 pictures before leaving a small crater on the floor of Alphonsus.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose, live on TV
fate.summary: Rangers had no brakes or landing legs. They were built to take TV pictures all the way down until they smashed into the Moon. Ranger 9 hit inside Alphonsus crater on March 24, 1965, at about 2.67 km per second, ending the Ranger program.

photo.caption: Ranger 7 at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in 1963. Ranger 9 was built to the same design (Rangers 6 to 9 were near-identical).

orbit.caption: The Ranger 9 impact site on the floor of Alphonsus crater, photographed from orbit by LRO's camera (image M117507817L).

lcross-centaur.summary: This was the empty Centaur upper stage of the rocket that launched NASA's LCROSS and LRO missions in June 2009. Instead of being left in space, it was steered into Cabeus, a crater near the Moon's south pole whose floor never sees sunlight. Its crash threw up a cloud of debris containing water ice, showing that the Moon's coldest craters hide frozen water.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose to hunt for ice
fate.summary: The Centaur was aimed at Cabeus crater so its impact would blast hidden material up into sunlight where instruments could study it. It hit on October 9, 2009, at about 2.5 km per second, while the LCROSS shepherding spacecraft followed behind to measure the plume.

photo.caption: This Centaur upper stage, lifted into its launch tower at Cape Canaveral in April 2009, launched LRO and LCROSS and later became the LCROSS impactor.

lcross-ssc.summary: The LCROSS shepherding spacecraft rode to the Moon attached to an empty Centaur rocket stage and guided it toward Cabeus crater near the south pole. After letting the Centaur go, it followed about four minutes behind, measuring the cloud of debris and detecting water before crashing into the same crater. It now lies in permanent darkness on the floor of Cabeus.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose after studying the plume
fate.summary: LCROSS separated from the Centaur about 10 hours before impact on October 9, 2009. It flew down through the debris plume with its cameras and instruments running, radioed the data home, and hit Cabeus itself about four minutes after the Centaur.

photo.caption: Workers pull back the protective cover from the LCROSS spacecraft at a processing facility in Florida in February 2009, four months before launch.

grail-ebb.summary: Ebb (GRAIL-A) was one of two identical spacecraft, each about the size of a washing machine, that chased each other around the Moon in 2012. By measuring tiny changes in the distance between them, the twins made the most detailed gravity map of any world at the time, revealing what lies beneath the Moon's surface. Ebb's mission ended with a planned crash into a mountain near the north pole, at a site named after astronaut Sally Ride.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose when fuel ran low
fate.summary: By December 2012 the twins were nearly out of fuel and their orbits were getting too low to keep flying. On December 17, 2012, NASA steered them into a mountain near Goldschmidt crater, a remote spot far from historic landing sites. Ebb hit first, at about 1.7 km per second.

photo.caption: Technicians prepare to lift Ebb (then called GRAIL-A) out of a vacuum test chamber in April 2011.

orbit.caption: The Ebb (GRAIL-A) impact site near the north pole, photographed from orbit by LRO's camera after the crash (image M1116736474R). The crater is only about 5 meters wide.

grail-flow.summary: Flow (GRAIL-B) was Ebb's twin, flying right behind it around the Moon so the pair could map the Moon's gravity in great detail. Students across the U.S. also used the twins' MoonKAM cameras to choose and take their own pictures of the Moon. Flow crashed into the same mountain as Ebb, at a site named after Sally Ride, the first American woman in space.

fate.label: Followed its twin into a planned crash
fate.summary: With fuel running low, both twins were deliberately crashed on December 17, 2012. Flow hit the mountain near Goldschmidt crater about 20 seconds after Ebb, and each left a crater about 5 meters across.

photo.caption: Flow (then called GRAIL-B) is lowered onto its launch adapter in Florida in August 2011, next to its twin Ebb (GRAIL-A) at right.

orbit.caption: The Flow (GRAIL-B) impact site near the north pole, photographed from orbit by LRO's camera after the crash (image M1116736474L). The crater is only about 5 meters wide.

ladee.summary: LADEE was a robot explorer that orbited the Moon in 2013 and 2014 to 'sniff' its extremely thin atmosphere and look for floating dust. It found gases such as neon, helium and argon, measured a thin cloud of dust kicked up by tiny meteorites, and tested sending data home by laser. Its mission ended with a crash on the far side of the Moon, where LRO later found its small crater.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose when fuel ran out
fate.summary: LADEE flew so low that it needed regular engine burns to stay in orbit, so its mission was always planned to end with a crash. With its fuel nearly gone, it hit the far side on April 18, 2014 (the evening of April 17 in U.S. time) at about 1.6 km per second.

photo.caption: LADEE during its spin test before launch in 2013. Engineers spun it at about one turn per second to check that it was perfectly balanced for flight.

orbit.caption: The LADEE impact site on the Moon's far side, photographed from orbit by LRO's camera (image M1163066820R). LADEE hit at a low angle, so its splash of bright debris has an hourglass shape.

lunar-prospector.summary: Lunar Prospector orbited the Moon for a year and a half, mapping what its surface is made of and measuring its gravity and magnetic fields. It found extra hydrogen near both poles, a hint that water ice is hiding in dark craters. At the end of its mission it was crashed into a shadowed crater near the south pole, now named Shoemaker, carrying some of the ashes of planetary scientist Eugene Shoemaker.

fate.label: Crashed on purpose to look for water
fate.summary: With its fuel running low, NASA used the last of it to steer Lunar Prospector into a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole on July 31, 1999. Scientists hoped the crash would throw up water vapor that telescopes on Earth and in space could spot, but no water was detected.

photo.caption: Technicians join Lunar Prospector to the rocket motor that would push it toward the Moon, at a processing facility in Florida in December 1997.
